questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Why vegetarians are healthier than meat eaters
Whether it's right to eat such clever plants
How to grow plants in dark places at home
Plants that catch and eat insects
questions.why: Neil asks: given the amazing things plants do, is it right to eat them?

questions.q: What is Rob's opinion at the start?
options: Eating plants is as bad as eating animals
Nobody should eat fruit
Plants can think and feel pain
Plants aren't alive in the same way as animals
questions.why: Rob says plants aren't alive in the same way as animals, and can't think or feel pain.

questions.q: According to some scientists, which of these can plants do?
options: Learn, remember and know their 'family'
Feel pain in the same way as animals
Move slowly from one place to another
Make loud sounds to warn nearby animals
questions.why: Neil says plants can learn and remember, solve problems and recognise other plants in their family.

questions.q: What does Professor Rick Karban say about plants' senses?
options: They can only sense light and nothing else
They sense much less than most animals
They sense as much as humans, and more
They need something like eyes to see light
questions.why: He agrees plants perceive most human senses 'and then some'.

questions.q: Why does Professor Karban mention dogs?
options: Because dogs often eat plants in gardens
To compare plants' chemical sense to dogs' noses
Because dogs were used in his experiments
To show that animals are cleverer than plants
questions.why: He says dogs have a much keener sense of smell than humans, and plants respond strongly to chemicals.

questions.q: What did the experiment with pea seedlings show?
options: They grew faster when music was played
They could talk to each other using roots
They needed less water than scientists expected
They learned and remembered the way to light
questions.why: They were trained to find the quickest route to light through a maze, and remember it.

questions.q: How did the lined-up potted plants pass information to each other?
options: Through their roots
Through their leaves
By releasing smells into the air
Through insects
questions.why: They passed information about water and air temperature through their roots.

questions.q: What is Professor Michael Marder's view?
options: Eating plants is always wrong
We should only eat plants we grow ourselves
It's fine, but think about which parts we take
Plants are not intelligent, so it doesn't matter
questions.why: He says it's not wrong in itself, but we should consider whether we destroy the whole plant or take parts like fruit.
